entry: American professional [[Skateboarding|skateboarder]], entrepreneur and owner of the skateboard company Birdhouse. A pioneer of modern vertical skateboarding, he completed the first documented "900" trick in 1999. Activision published a skateboarding video game series named after him that same year. Hawk, who was born in [[San Diego]], [[California]], retired from professional competition in 2003 and is active in the Skatepark Project, which helps build skateparks in underprivileged areas around the world.

American rock band formed in [[Los Angeles]] in 1990. Its members are vocalist Maynard James Keenan, guitarist Adam Jones, drummer Danny Carey and bassist Justin Chancellor, who replaced founding member Paul D'Amour in 1995. With *Ænima* (1996), the band became a dominant act in alternative and progressive metal. Its albums *Lateralus* (2001) and *10,000 Days* (2006) drew critical acclaim, and Tool has won four [[Grammy Awards]]. The band combines music with [[Visual arts|visual art]] and themes of personal evolution. Its relationship with the music industry is ambivalent, at times marked by [[Censorship|censorship]], and it insists on privacy.

Hard, calcified structure in the jaws or mouths of many [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], used to break down food. Some animals, particularly [[Carnivore|carnivores]], also use teeth to capture or wound prey, tear food and defend themselves. Teeth are not made of bone; they consist of tissues of varying density and hardness that originate from the ectoderm, the outermost embryonic germ layer. Most [[Mammal|mammals]], including [[Human|humans]], are diphyodonts, growing one set of deciduous teeth followed by permanent teeth. Elephants, kangaroos and [[Manatee|manatees]] are polyphyodonts, growing many sets over their lives, and sharks grow a new set every two weeks. Rodent incisors grow and wear away continually through gnawing, and voles and [[Guinea pig|guinea pigs]] (but not mice) also have continuously growing molars. Among reptiles, teeth are generally simple and conical, with the venom-injecting fangs of [[Snake|snakes]] a notable exception.

Breakdown of teeth due to acids produced by [[Bacteria|bacteria]], also known as caries or dental cavities. Bacteria produce acid from food debris and sugar on the tooth surface, dissolving enamel, dentin and cementum. Simple sugars are the bacteria's main energy source, so a diet high in them is a risk factor. Caries results when demineralization outpaces remineralization from sources such as saliva. Risk factors include conditions that reduce saliva, such as [[Diabetes|diabetes]] mellitus, and medications including [[Stimulant|psychostimulants]], antihistamines and antidepressants. Prevention relies on fluoride, a low-sugar diet, and regular brushing and flossing. Treatment depends on the extent of destruction, and no known method regrows large amounts of tooth. [[Paracetamol]] or [[Ibuprofen|ibuprofen]] may be taken for pain. As of 2016, approximately 3.6 billion people (48% of the global population) had caries in their permanent teeth.

British motoring-themed magazine television program. The [[BBC]] revived it in 2002 after a 1977–2001 run. Devised by [[Jeremy Clarkson]] and Andy Wilman, it premiered on October 20, 2002, and added motoring challenges and races. Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May were the core presenters, with the anonymous test driver "The Stig." In March 2015 the BBC chose not to renew Clarkson's contract after an incident during filming; Hammond and May left with him for [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]]'s *The Grand Tour*. In August 2026 the BBC announced the show would return, without confirming hosts.

Silicate [[Mineral|mineral]] containing aluminum and [[Fluorine|fluorine]], used as a [[Gemstone|gemstone]]. Common topaz is colorless in its natural state, though trace impurities can make it pale blue or golden-brown to yellow-orange. It is often treated with heat or radiation to produce deep blue, reddish-orange, pale green, pink or purple colors. It is one of the hardest naturally occurring minerals, and major sources include Brazil and Russia. Many English Bible translations, including the [[King James Version]], mention topaz, but they derive from a [[Septuagint]] term for a yellow stone that was probably chrysolite, so topaz is likely not meant.

City (pop., 2020: 126,587), capital of [[Kansas]] and county seat of Shawnee County. The city was laid out in 1854 as a Free-State town by Eastern antislavery men. Its name is a Kansa-Osage word meaning roughly "a good place to dig potatoes." A [[Ferry|ferry]] service across the Kansas River served travelers on the [[Oregon Trail]] at the site. Steamboats delivered meat, lumber and flour and returned with potatoes, corn and wheat. Topeka is known for the Supreme Court case *Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka*, which overturned *Plessy v. Ferguson* and declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional.

State of a woman's [[Breast|breasts]] being exposed, including areolas and [[Nipple|nipples]], especially in public or visual media. Social norms vary: many Indigenous societies consider breast exposure normal, and some beaches in Europe and Australia allow topless sunbathing. In most countries, however, norms of female modesty require women to cover their breasts in public, and many jurisdictions prosecute public toplessness as indecent exposure. The topfreedom movement opposes such laws on grounds of [[Gender equality|gender equality]]. Toplessness appears often in painting, sculpture, film and photography, where it is often defended on artistic grounds, and features prominently in [[Erotica|erotica]] and [[Pornography|pornography]].

Height of a summit above the lowest contour line encircling it that contains no higher summit, a measure of independence. Prominence is the least drop in height needed to get from a summit to higher terrain. The key col is the highest of the lowest points on all paths to higher ground. [[K2]], the second-highest mountain, has a prominence of 4,017 m. The South Summit of [[Mount Everest]] is taller, at 8,749 m, but its prominence is only 11 m, so it is not regarded as an independent mountain. Peaks with high prominence are likely to have extraordinary views.

Set equipped with a topology, a structure defining closeness among its points without a numeric [[Distance|distance]]. A topology is most commonly defined through [[Open set|open sets]], though it can also be defined by a set of neighborhoods for each point that satisfy axioms of closeness. Topological spaces are the most general setting in which limits, continuity and connectedness can be defined. Common examples include [[Euclidean space|Euclidean spaces]], [[Metric space|metric spaces]] and [[Manifold|manifolds]]. The study of topological spaces in their own right is called general topology, or point-set topology. Felix Hausdorff first defined topological spaces in 1914 in his *Principles of Set Theory*, and the concept is fundamental to virtually every branch of modern [[Mathematics|mathematics]].

Free, open-source overlay network for anonymous communication, based on onion routing. Volunteer-operated relays, numbering over seven thousand, route users' traffic along random paths, so no single point on the [[Internet]] can see both where traffic originates and where it is going. Onion routing was developed in the mid-1990s by employees of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, and the network's code was released under a free license in 2004. The [[Massachusetts]]-based nonprofit Tor Project, founded in 2006, maintains it. Users range from activists to criminal enterprises and law enforcement agencies.

Compilation of the first five books of the [[Hebrew Bible]], namely Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, central to [[Judaism]]. The word means "instruction" or "teaching," and the translation "law" is considered misleading. Rabbinic tradition holds that God gave the Torah through [[Moses]], who wrote it down, and that the Oral Torah, embodied in the [[Talmud]], consists of interpretations and amplifications. A Torah scroll is written by a scribe in Hebrew, and a portion is read publicly in a [[Synagogue|synagogue]] on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays. Muslims believe God gave the Torah to the prophets, and it is also part of the Christian [[Old Testament]]. Biblical scholarship generally regards the final form of the Torah as largely complete by the Persian period, though this is widely debated.

Violently rotating column of air extending from the surface of the [[Earth]] to the base of a [[Cumulonimbus cloud|cumulonimbus]] or [[Cumulus cloud|cumulus]] cloud. Most tornadoes have wind speeds below 180 km per hour (110 mph), are about 80 m (250 ft) across and travel a few miles before dissipating; the most extreme exceed 480 km per hour (300 mph). The United States has by far the most tornadoes of any country, concentrated in "Tornado Alley." Intensity is rated on the Fujita scale, replaced in some countries by the Enhanced Fujita Scale, from EF0, which damages trees, to EF5, which can rip buildings off their foundations. Over water, [[Waterspout|waterspouts]] are generally classified as non-supercellular tornadoes.

Most populous city in [[Canada]] and capital of [[Ontario]], on the northwestern shore of [[Lake Ontario]] (pop., 2021: 2,794,356). Indigenous peoples have lived in the area for more than 10,000 years. The British established the town of York in 1793, and during the [[War of 1812]] it was occupied for two weeks by American troops. York was renamed and incorporated as the City of Toronto in 1834, and it became the capital of Ontario in 1867. The Greater Toronto Area has a population of 6,712,341. About half of its residents were born outside Canada, and over 200 ethnic origins are represented. Toronto is Canada's largest financial center and home to the Toronto Stock Exchange. It is the fourth-most populous city in North America, behind [[Mexico City]], [[New York City]] and [[Los Angeles]].

Professional [[Ice hockey|ice hockey]] team based in [[Toronto]] and a member of the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL). Founded as the Toronto Arenas for the 1917–18 NHL season, it was renamed the Maple Leafs by Conn Smythe after he bought it in 1927. The club has won more Stanley Cup championships than any NHL team other than the [[Montreal Canadiens]]. Its dynasties from 1946–47 to 1950–51 and from 1961–62 to 1966–67 won a combined eight of eleven Stanley Cups. The championship drought that followed, at 57 seasons, is the longest in league history. The team plays at Scotiabank Arena.

Self-propelled underwater weapon launched from above or below the water surface, with an explosive warhead for contact or proximity detonation. The word first named [[Electric ray|electric rays]], and the term originally covered many devices now called [[Naval mine|mines]]. In 1866 Robert Whitehead developed the first practical self-propelled torpedo, at Fiume in [[Austria-Hungary]]. From the 1860s onward, torpedoes allowed small [[Submarine|submarines]], torpedo boats and even light [[Aircraft|aircraft]] to destroy large ships without large guns. Modern torpedoes are lightweight or heavyweight, straight-running, homing or wire-guided, and can be launched from many platforms. In modern warfare, a submarine-launched torpedo is almost certain to hit its target, and the best defense is a counterattack with another torpedo.

Rotational equivalent of linear [[Force|force]], a twist applied to an object about an axis, also called the moment of force. Torque is the product of the perpendicular component of a force and the distance from the axis to the line of action, known as the [[Lever|lever]] arm. In vector form it is the [[Cross product|cross product]] of the position and force vectors, with direction given by the [[Right-hand rule|right-hand rule]]. Its SI unit is the newton-meter (N·m). Torque causes angular acceleration in rigid bodies, appearing in applications from levers and pulleys to [[Engine|engines]]. The term comes from the Latin *torquēre*, "to twist," and was suggested by James Thomson, appearing in print in 1884. In mechanical engineering in the UK and the U.S., it is usually called the moment of force, a usage traced to [[Siméon Denis Poisson]] in 1811.

Civil wrong, other than breach of [[Contract|contract]], causing loss or harm to a claimant and resulting in legal liability. Tort law aims to compensate victims, whereas [[Criminal law|criminal law]] aims to punish individuals who commit crimes. Some acts, such as [[Assault|assault]] and [[Battery (crime)|battery]], can result in both a civil lawsuit and a criminal prosecution. The main remedy is [[Damages|damages]], or money, though courts may also grant an injunction. Common law jurisdictions derive tort law from English custom and precedent, while [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] jurisdictions largely derive it from Roman law. Some countries, including the [[Philippines]] and [[Thailand]], have codified a mixture of common and civil law. The word was first used in a legal context in the 1580s.

Land-dwelling [[Turtle|turtle]] of the family Testudinidae, a [[Reptile|reptile]] with a hard shell that protects it from [[Predation|predation]] and retracts its head and neck into the shell. Tortoise species vary widely in size. The [[Galápagos tortoise]] exceeds 1.2 m (3.9 ft) in length, while the speckled Cape tortoise's shell measures only 6.8 cm (2.7 in). Several lineages independently evolved bodies over 100 kg (220 lb). Tortoises are the longest-living land animals, and Galápagos tortoises are noted to live over 150 years, while most species live 80–150 years. In 1968 two Russian tortoises aboard *Zond 5* became the first Earthlings to circle the Moon. Most species seldom lay more than 20 eggs, and incubation averages 100 to 160 days.

Deliberate infliction of severe pain or suffering on a person to punish, extract a confession, gather information or intimidate third parties. Some definitions restrict torture to acts by the [[State (polity)|state]], while others include non-state actors. Most victims are poor and marginalized people suspected of crimes. Torturers more often act out of fear or limited resources than sadism, and beating is the most common physical method. Since the twentieth century, many torturers have preferred non-scarring or psychological methods. Torture can cause chronic pain and mental harm, and survivors have some of the highest rates of [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]]. Many Western countries abolished official judicial torture in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It is prohibited under [[International law]] for all states in all circumstances, and opposition to it helped stimulate the [[Human rights|human rights]] movement after [[World War II]]. Despite its decline, torture is still practiced in or by most countries.

Doughnut-shaped [[Geometry|geometric]] surface generated by rotating a [[Circle|circle]] one full revolution about an axis coplanar with it. If the axis does not touch the circle, the result is a ring torus, sometimes called a doughnut. A horn torus results when the axis is tangent to the circle, and a spindle torus when the axis passes twice through it. Real-world approximations of a ring torus include swim rings and inner tubes. In [[Topology|topology]], a ring torus is homeomorphic to the Cartesian product of two circles, a compact 2-[[Manifold|manifold]] of genus 1.

Japanese actor and film producer, noted for hypermasculine or heroic roles. He appeared in more than 180 screen credits, including 16 films with director [[Akira Kurosawa]], among them *Rashomon* (1950) and *[[Seven Samurai]]* (1954). He won Best Actor at the Venice Film Festival for *Yojimbo* (1961) and again for *Red Beard* (1965). He played [[Miyamoto Musashi]] in the *Samurai Trilogy* (1954–1956) and Admiral [[Isoroku Yamamoto]] in three films. In 1962 he established Mifune Productions, which achieved success with large-scale works such as *The Sands of Kurobe* (1968). He later worked in Hollywood, debuting in *Grand Prix* (1966). In 2016 his name was inscribed on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Form of government that completely controls public and private life, prohibits opposing political parties and suppresses opposition to the state. A totalitarian government uses an ideology to control the economy, education, the arts and sciences, and the private morality of its citizens. The difference from [[Authoritarianism|authoritarian]] rule is one of degree: totalitarianism features a charismatic dictator and a fixed worldview. The word was first used in the early 1920s to describe Italy's Fascist government. During the early [[Cold War]], it came to compare the [[Soviet Union]] under [[Joseph Stalin]] with [[Nazi Germany]] under [[Adolf Hitler]]. Some historians have challenged the concept, arguing that total control was never achieved and that Nazism and Stalinism differed substantially. In the 21st century the term has also been applied to [[Islamism|Islamist]] movements, a use that is also contested.

Spirit being, sacred object or symbol serving as an emblem of a group, such as a family, [[Clan|clan]], lineage or tribe. The word comes from the [[Ojibwe]] term *doodem*. Anishinaabe peoples are divided into clans named mainly for animal totems, such as bear, crane and moose. Belief in tutelary spirits is not limited to the Ojibwe, and similar concepts appear in cultures worldwide. Totem poles of the [[Pacific Northwest]] are carved monuments that may serve as crests of families or chiefs, recount stories or commemorate events. Many [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal Australian]] and Torres Strait Islander groups object to the imported term, and some use "token" instead. Some contemporary [[New Age]] and men's movements use "totem" for personal identification with a tutelary spirit.

Neotropical [[Bird|bird]] of the family Ramphastidae, marked by large, often colorful bills. The family includes five genera and over 40 species, including aracaris and toucanets, and its closest relatives are the toucan-barbets. Toucans are arboreal and usually found in pairs or small flocks. They nest in tree hollows, often excavated by [[Woodpecker|woodpeckers]], and typically lay two to four white eggs. The bill is very light, built of bone struts filled with foam-like keratin, and it also serves as an efficient [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulation]] system. Early naturalists thought toucans were carnivorous, but they eat mostly fruit. In Africa and Asia, [[Hornbill|hornbills]] occupy the same [[Ecological niche|ecological niche]], an example of convergent evolution.
